nodes.name: Real vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Throughout the text, $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the $n$-dimensional linear real vector space.

nodes.name: Inner product in $\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Unless stated otherwise, symbols $\boldsymbol{x}_i=(x_{i,1},\dots,x_{i,n})$ denote elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\big(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j\big)=\sum_{k} x_{i,k} x_{j,k}$ is the inner product of $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_j$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Points $\boldsymbol{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and the standard inner product $(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j)=\sum_k x_{i,k}x_{j,k}$.

nodes.name: Unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$
nodes.statement: Symbol $\mathbb{B}_n$ stands for the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ centered at the origin: $\mathbb{B}_n=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n| \ \left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}\right)\leq 1\}$.
nodes.genus: unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ centered at the origin

nodes.name: Linearly separable set
nodes.statement: A set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is {\em linearly separable} if for each $x\in S$ there exists a linear functional $l$ such that $l(x)>l(y)$ for all $y\in S$, $y\neq x$.
differentia: for each $x\in S$ there exists a linear functional $l$ such that $l(x)>l(y)$ for all $y\in S$, $y\neq x$
nodes.statement_short: Every point of $S$ can be strictly separated from the rest of $S$ by a linear functional.

nodes.name: Extreme point
nodes.statement: Recall that $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is an {\em extreme point} of a convex compact $K$ if there exist no points $y,z\in K$, $y\neq z$ such that $x=(y+z)/2$.
differentia: there exist no points $y,z\in K$, $y\neq z$ such that $x=(y+z)/2$

nodes.name: Basic examples of linearly separable sets
nodes.statement: The basic examples of linearly separable sets are extreme points of a convex compacts: vertices of convex polyhedra or points on the $n$-dimensional sphere.

nodes.name: Extreme points need not be linearly separable
nodes.statement: The sets of extreme points of a compact may be not linearly separable as is demonstrated by simple 2D examples \citep{Simon2011}.

nodes.name: Linearly separable sets are extreme points
nodes.statement: Every compact linearly separable set $S \subset \mathbb{ R}^n$ is a set of extreme points of a convex compact $K={\rm conv} S$.
conclusions: is a set of extreme points of a convex compact $K={\rm conv} S$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: The proof follows immediately from the previous definitions, the Krein-Milman theorem \citep{Simon2011} (its finite-dimensional form was known to Minkovsky) and classical theorems about separation of a point from a convex set.
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the definitions, the Krein-Milman theorem and separation of a point from a convex set.

nodes.name: Heuristic: simplex volume suggests separability of large random sets
nodes.statement: If $n+1$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ do not belong to a hyperplane then they are vertices of a simplex and are, obviously, linearly separable. If the lengths of the edges are bounded then the volume of the simplex decreases with $n$ not slower than $1/n!$. Therefore, we can expect that for a sufficiently regular distribution of points, a random point does not belong to the simplex, and $n+2$ independently chosen random points are also linearly separable, with high probability, which tends to 1 as $1-c/n!$ ($n\to \infty$, $ c>0$). This fast convergence allows us to hypothesize that even a large random finite set is linearly separable in high dimension with high probability, if the distribution is regular enough.
nodes.statement_short: Simplex volume decays like $1/n!$, so random points are likely outside the simplex of others; motivates separability of large random sets.

nodes.name: Probability of the outer spherical layer
nodes.statement: Let us start from the equidistribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. The probability $p$ that a random point belongs to a layer $\mathbb{B}_n \setminus r\mathbb{ B}_n$ ($0<r<1$) between spheres of radius 1 and of radius $r$ is $p=1-r^n$.
conclusions: The probability $p$ that a random point belongs to a layer $\mathbb{B}_n \setminus r\mathbb{ B}_n$ ($0<r<1$) between spheres of radius 1 and of radius $r$ is $p=1-r^n$.

nodes.name: Spherical cap bound
nodes.statement: Let us take a unit vector $ \boldsymbol{v}$. The probability that the projection of a random vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ on $ \boldsymbol{v}$, $( \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{v})$, exceeds $r$ can be estimated from above by half of the ratio of volumes of balls of radii $\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and 1 (see Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with $\varepsilon=1-r$): $ \mathbf{P}(( \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{v})>r)\leq 0.5 \rho^{n}$.
assumptions: Let us take a unit vector $ \boldsymbol{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: For a unit vector $v$, $P((x,v)>r)\le 0.5\rho^n$ with $\rho=\sqrt{1-r^2}$, by comparing cap and ball volumes.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: The proof is based on the independence of random points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$, on the geometric picture presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}, and on an elementary inequality $\mathbf{P}(A_1 \& A_2 \& \ldots \& A_m)\geq 1- \sum_i(1-\mathbf{P}(A_i))$ for any events $A_1, \ldots , A_m$. In Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} we should take $\varepsilon=1-r$ and the external radius of the spherical layer $A$ is 1.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over the independent points, using the spherical layer and cap geometry of Fig. 1.

nodes.name: Sample-size estimates for the unit ball (Corollary 1)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ and $0<r,\vartheta<1$. If \begin{equation} M<2({\vartheta-r^n})/{\rho^{n}}, \end{equation} then $ \mathbf{P}((\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_M{)}<r\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\| \mbox{ for all } i=1,\ldots, M-1)>1-\vartheta. $ If \begin{equation} M<({r}/{\rho})^n\left(-1+\sqrt{1+{2 \vartheta \rho^n}/{r^{2n}}}\right), \end{equation} then $\mathbf{P}((\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j)<r\|\boldsymbol{x}_i\| \mbox{ for all } i,j=1,\ldots, M, \, i\neq j)\geq 1-\vartheta.$ In particular, if inequality (\ref{EstimateM2ball}) holds then the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
assumptions: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points  from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ and $0<r,\vartheta<1$.
conclusions: $\mathbf{P}((\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j)<r\|\boldsymbol{x}_i\| \mbox{ for all } i,j=1,\ldots, M, \, i\neq j)\geq 1-\vartheta.$
the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit exponential-in-$n$ bounds on $M$ under which the separation events of Theorem 1 hold with probability $>1-\vartheta$.

nodes.label: EstimateM2ball

nodes.statement: A weaker and simpler estimate (sufficient condition) follows immediately from (\ref{EstimateM2ball}): \begin{equation} {\vartheta}/ M^2>{r^n+0.5\rho^{n}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\vartheta/M^2>r^n+0.5\rho^n$ suffices for (5).

nodes.statement: {\vartheta}/ M^2>{r^n+0.5\rho^{n}}.

nodes.name: Remark 1: 2,700,000 points in dimension 100
nodes.statement: According to (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) the pre exponential factor in the estimate for $M^2$ may be chosen as $\vartheta $, while the exponent depends on $r$ only. For example, for $r=1/\sqrt{2}$ the simple sufficient condition (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) gives $M^2<\frac{2}{3}\vartheta 2^{n/2}$. For $\vartheta=0.01$ (or specificity 99\%) and $n=100$ we get $M<2,740,000$. Thus, if we select 2,700,000 i.i.d. points from an equidistribution in a unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^{100} $ then with probability $p>0.99$ {\em all} these points will be vertices of their convex hull.
nodes.statement_short: With $r=1/\sqrt2$, $\vartheta=0.01$, $n=100$: up to 2,700,000 uniform points in the ball are all vertices of their convex hull with probability $>0.99$.

nodes.name: Estimates apply to the unit sphere with margins
nodes.statement: Estimates similar to (\ref{Eq:ballMangle}), (\ref{EstimateM2ball}), and (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}) are useful for the equidistribution of the normalized data on a unit sphere too. This is because they not only establish the fact of separability but also specify separation margins.

nodes.name: Product distribution in a unit cube
nodes.statement: Consider a product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube. Let the coordinates of a random point, $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ ($0 \leq X_i \leq 1$) be independent random variables with expectations $\overline{X}_i$ and variances $\sigma_i^2>\sigma_0^2>0$.
nodes.definiendum: product distribution in an $n$-dimensional unit cube
differentia: the coordinates of a random point, $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ ($0 \leq X_i \leq 1$) be independent random variables with expectations $\overline{X}_i$ and variances $\sigma_i^2>\sigma_0^2>0$
nodes.statement_short: Coordinates are independent random variables in $[0,1]$ with means $\overline X_i$ and variances bounded below by $\sigma_0^2$.

nodes.name: Mean vector $\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}$
nodes.statement: Let $\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}$ be a vector with coordinates $\overline{X}_i$.

nodes.name: Concentration near spheres of radius R
nodes.statement: For large $n$, this distribution is concentrated in a relatively small vicinity of a sphere with an {\em arbitrary} centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ with coordinates $c_i$ and radius $R$, where \begin{equation} R^2=\mathbf{E}\left(\sum_i (X_i-c_i)^2\right)=\sum_i \sigma_i^2 + \|\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{c}\|^2. \end{equation}
conclusions: this distribution is concentrated in a relatively small vicinity of a sphere with an {\em arbitrary} centre $\boldsymbol{c}$ with coordinates $c_i$ and radius $R$
nodes.statement_short: The product distribution concentrates near a sphere around any centre $c$ with radius $R^2=\sum_i\sigma_i^2+\|\overline x-c\|^2$.

nodes.name: Concentration radius (7)
nodes.statement: R^2=\mathbf{E}\left(\sum_i (X_i-c_i)^2\right)=\sum_i \sigma_i^2 + \|\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{c}\|^2.
nodes.label: ConcRad

nodes.name: Hoeffding inequality
nodes.statement: Let $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be independent bounded random variables: $0 \leq Y_i \leq 1$. The empirical mean of these variables is defined as $\overline Y = \frac{1}{n}(Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n)$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right); \\ &\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right). \end{split} \end{equation}
assumptions: Let  $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$ be independent bounded random variables: $0 \leq Y_i \leq 1$.
conclusions: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right); \\ &\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right). \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Tail of the empirical mean of independent $[0,1]$ variables decays as $\exp(-2nt^2)$.

nodes.name: Equation (8)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \geq t \right) \leq \exp \left(-2n t^2 \right); \\ &\mathbf{P} \left(\left |\overline Y - \mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right] \right | \geq t \right) \leq 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right). \end{split}

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let us take $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$. Consider the centres located in the cube, $0\leq c_i \leq 1$. Then $0\leq Y_i \leq 1$ and $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R^2$. In particular, if $c_i=\overline{X}_i$ then $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R_0^2$ (the minimal possible value), where $R_0^2=\sum_i \sigma_i^2\geq n\sigma_0^2$. In general, $n\sigma_0^2\leq R^2 \leq n$. With probability $p>1- 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ a random point $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to the spherical layer ($\delta={nt}/{R_0^2}$, $t=\delta R_0^2/n$): \begin{equation} 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta. \end{equation} Consider $M$ i.i.d. points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ from the product distribution. With probability $p>1- 2M\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ they all belong to the spherical layer (\ref{sphericLayer}). Therefore, with this probability we return to the situation presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with internal radius $\sqrt{1-\delta}R_0$ and external radius $\sqrt{1+\delta}R_0$. The difference from the equidistribution in the ball is that the volume of the ball is concentrated near the external sphere, while the distribution in the layer (\ref{sphericLayer}) is concentrated around the sphere $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2=R_0^2$. The radius of ball $B$ is defined by $\rho^2=(1+\delta)R_0^2-(1-\delta)R_0^2=2\delta R_0^2$. The concentration radius (\ref{ConcRad}) for the spheres concentric with the ball $B$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) is defined by $R^2=R_0^2+(1-\delta)R_0^2=(2-\delta)R_0^2$. Therefore, a random point does not belong to the ball $B$ with probability $p>1- \exp \left(-2n\tau^2 \right)$, where $\tau=\frac{1}{n}(R^2-\rho^2)=\frac{1}{n}(2-3 \delta)R^2_0$. Thus, we get the following statement.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Hoeffding to $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ to put all points in a thin spherical layer, then bound the probability of landing in the separating ball $B$ by Hoeffding again.

nodes.name: Spherical layer (9)
nodes.statement: 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta.
nodes.label: sphericLayer

nodes.name: Stochastic separation theorem for product distributions in a cube (Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points from the product distribution in a unit cube, $0< \delta <2/3$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right); \end{split} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -M(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right) \end{split} \end{equation}
assumptions: Let  $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points  from the product distribution in a unit cube, $0< \delta <2/3$.
conclusions: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right); \end{split}

\begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -M(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right) \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: For i.i.d. points from a product distribution in the cube, all points lie in a thin layer around $\overline x$ and are mutually separated, with probability $1-O(M^2 e^{-cR_0^4/n})$.
nodes.label: cube

nodes.name: Equation (10)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right); \end{split}
nodes.label: Eq:cube1

nodes.name: Equation (11)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(1-\delta \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq 1+\delta \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1- 2M\exp \left(-2\delta^2 R_0^4/n \right) -M(M-1)\exp \left(-2R_0^4(2-3 \delta)^2/n\right) \end{split}
nodes.label: Eq:cube2

nodes.name: Theorem 2 estimates for $\delta=0.5$
nodes.statement: When the value of delta is chosen as $\delta=0.5$ and $R_0$ is replaced with its estimate from below, $R^2_0\geq n \sigma_0^2$, inequalities (\ref{Eq:cube1}) and (\ref{Eq:cube2}) result in the following estimates: \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq \frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1-3M\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right); \end{split} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq\frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1-M(M+1)\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right). \end{split} \end{equation}
assumptions: the value of delta is chosen as $\delta=0.5$ and $R_0$ is replaced with its estimate from below, $R^2_0\geq n \sigma_0^2$
conclusions: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq \frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1-3M\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right); \end{split}

\begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq\frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1-M(M+1)\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right). \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: With $\delta=0.5$ and $R_0^2\ge n\sigma_0^2$, the failure probabilities become $3M e^{-0.5n\sigma_0^4}$ and $M(M+1)e^{-0.5n\sigma_0^4}$.

nodes.name: Equation (12)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq \frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ & \left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq M \right)\\ &\geq 1-3M\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right); \end{split}
nodes.label: Eq:cube3

nodes.name: Equation (13)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R^2_0}\leq\frac{3}{2} \mbox{ and } \right. \\ &\left. \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\| }\right)<\sqrt{1-\delta} \mbox{ for all } i,j, \, i\neq j \right)\\ &\geq 1-M(M+1)\exp\left(-0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right). \end{split}
nodes.label: Eq:cube4

nodes.name: Sample-size estimates for the cube (Corollary 2)
nodes.statement: Let $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points from the product distribution in a unit cube and $0<\vartheta<1$. If \begin{equation} M<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right), \end{equation} then with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ \[ \begin{split} & 0.5\leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R_0^2} \leq 1.5 \mbox{ and } \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|}\right)<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ &\mbox{ for all } i,j, i \neq M. \end{split} \] If \begin{equation} (M+1)^2<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right), \end{equation} then with probability $p>1-\vartheta$ \[ \begin{split} &0.5\leq \frac{\|\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}{R_0^2} \leq 1.5 \mbox{ and } \left(\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_i-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{R_0},\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_j-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|}\right)<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ & \mbox{ for all }i,j, i\neq j. \end{split} \] In particular, if inequality (\ref{SampleSizeCube2}) holds then the set $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
assumptions: Let  $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be i.i.d. random points  from the product distribution in a unit cube and $0<\vartheta<1$.
conclusions: the set   $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ is linearly separable with probability $p>1-\vartheta$.
nodes.statement_short: If $M$ (resp. $(M+1)^2$) is below $\frac13\vartheta e^{0.5n\sigma_0^4}$, one point (resp. every point) is separated from the rest with probability $>1-\vartheta$.

nodes.name: Equation (14)
nodes.statement: M<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right),
nodes.label: SampleSizeCube1

nodes.name: Equation (15)
nodes.statement: (M+1)^2<\frac{1}{3}\vartheta \exp\left(0.5 n\sigma_0^4 \right),
nodes.label: SampleSizeCube2

nodes.name: Numerical experiments on separability in the unit cube
nodes.statement: The estimates (\ref{SampleSizeCube1}), (\ref{SampleSizeCube2}) are far from being optimal and can be improved. The main message here is their exponential dependence on $n$: the upper boundary of $M$ can grow with $n$ exponentially. Numerical experiments show that the equidistribution in cube is not worse, from the practical point of view, than the uniform distribution in a ball. To illustrate this, we empirically assessed linear separability of samples drawn from equidistributions in the unit $n$-cubes. For selected values of $n$ from the set $\{1,\dots,5000\}$ we generated $100$ samples $S$ of $M=20 000$ random points from $[0,1]^n$. For each sample, a sub-sample $\underline{S}\subset S$ of $N=4000$ points was randomly chosen, and for each point $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ in this sub-sample linear functionals $l(\boldsymbol{x})=\left(\boldsymbol{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}},\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}}\right)-\|\boldsymbol{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\bar{x}}\|^{2}$ were constructed. Sings of $l(\boldsymbol{x}_j)$, $\boldsymbol{x}_j\in S$, $\boldsymbol{x}_j\neq \boldsymbol{x}_i$ were calculated, and the numbers $N_{-}$ of instances when $l(\boldsymbol{x}_j)< 0$ where recorded. Empirical frequencies $N_{-}/N$ were then derived. Outcomes of this experiment are summarized in Fig. \ref{fig:experiments_cube}. These experiments demonstrate that the probability that a randomly selected point in a sample is linearly separable from the rest could be significantly higher than the simple exponential estimates provided. This, however, is not surprising as the estimates are based on the values of means and variances, and do not take into account other quantitative properties of the sample distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Experiments with 20,000 uniform points in $[0,1]^n$ show separability frequencies far above the exponential estimates.

nodes.name: Two-neuron separability
nodes.statement: In general position, a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ is linearly separable. Therefore, if $n-1$ or less points from $\mathcal{M}=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_{M-1}\}$ are not separated from $\boldsymbol{x}$ by the hyperplane $L$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) then they can be separated by an additional hyperplane orthogonal to $L$. This means that $\boldsymbol{x}$ can be separated from the whole $\mathcal{M}$ by a conjunction of two linear inequalities, $(\bullet , \boldsymbol{x}/\|\boldsymbol{x}\|) >r \, \& \, (\bullet , \boldsymbol{y}) > q$, for some $0<r<0$, $q>0$, and $\boldsymbol{y}$, $(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})=0$. This system can be considered as a cascade of two independent neurons \citep{GorbanRomBurtTyu2016}. The probability of such a {\em two-neuron separability} is higher than of linear separability. (Compare inequality (\ref{Eq:ball1n}) in the following theorem to (\ref{Eq:ball1}).)
nodes.statement_short: A point not linearly separable from at most $n-1$ others can be separated by a conjunction of two linear inequalities (a two-neuron cascade).

nodes.name: Two-neuron (cascade) separation theorem for the unit ball (Theorem 3)
nodes.statement: Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$ i.i.d. random points from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$, $0<r<1$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \, \&\, \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \mbox{ points } \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \\ & \geq (1-r^n)(1-0.5\rho^{n})^{M-1} \\ &\times \left(1-\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right)^n\right) \exp{\left[\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right]}, \end{split} \end{equation}
assumptions: Let $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ be a set of $M$  i.i.d. random points  from the equidustribution in the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$, $0<r<1$.
conclusions: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \, \&\, \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \mbox{ points } \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \\ & \geq (1-r^n)(1-0.5\rho^{n})^{M-1} \\ &\times \left(1-\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right)^n\right) \exp{\left[\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right]}, \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on the probability that $x_M$ is separated by the hyperplane from all but at most $n$ of the other uniform points in the ball.
nodes.label: CascadeSep

nodes.name: Equation (16)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \, \&\, \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \mbox{ points } \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \\ & \geq (1-r^n)(1-0.5\rho^{n})^{M-1} \\ &\times \left(1-\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right)^n\right) \exp{\left[\frac{0.5(M-n)\rho^{n}}{1-0.5\rho^{n}}\right]}, \end{split}
nodes.label: Eq:ball1n

nodes.name: Numerical evaluation of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: For $r=1/\sqrt{2}$, $n=100$, and $M=2,74\cdot 10^6$, (\ref{Eq:ball1n}) gives: $\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \& \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \ \ \boldsymbol{x}_i\ \in S\right) \geq 1-\theta$ with $\theta<5\cdot 10^{-14}$. The probability stays close to $1$ for much larger values of $M$, as setting $M=7\cdot 10^{16}$ results in the estimate: $\mathbf{P} \left(\|\boldsymbol{x}_M\|>r \& \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i,\frac{\boldsymbol{x}_M}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_M\| }\right)<r \mbox{ for at least } M\!-\!n \ \ \boldsymbol{x}_i\in S\right) \geq 1-\theta$ with $\theta<5\cdot 10^{-9}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=100$, (16) gives failure probability below $5\cdot10^{-14}$ at $M=2.74\cdot10^6$ and below $5\cdot10^{-9}$ at $M=7\cdot10^{16}$.

nodes.name: Weakly dependent coordinates
nodes.statement: Relax the requirement of independent coordinates in Theorem~\ref{cube} to that of weakly dependent vector-valued variables;

nodes.name: Strongly log-concave distributions
nodes.statement: Instead of equidistributions, consider distributions with strongly log-concave probability densities;

nodes.name: Nonlinear classifiers and VC dimension
nodes.statement: Use various simple and robust nonlinear classifiers like small neural cascades (compare to Theorem~\ref{CascadeSep}), algebraic classifiers and other families. For these generalisations, the VC dimension is expected to play the role similar to dimension $n$ in Theorems \ref{ball1point} and \ref{cube}.

nodes.name: Stochastic separation and one-shot correction of AI systems
nodes.statement: Stochastic separation Theorems 1--3 are important for synthesis and one-shot correction of AI systems. For example, inequalities (\ref{ball1point}) and (\ref{Eq:cube1}) evaluate the probability that a randomly selected point $\boldsymbol{x}_M$ is linearly separable from all other $M-1$ points by the linear functional $l(\boldsymbol{x})=(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_M-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}})$. This separation is sufficient to correct a mistake of a legacy AI system without any re-learning and modification of existing skills \citep{GorbanRomBurtTyu2016}.
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 1-3 bound the probability that a point is separated from the rest by $l(x)=(x,x_M-\overline x)$, enough to correct a legacy AI error without retraining.

nodes.name: Separability in the Mahalanobis inner product
nodes.statement: For example, according to (\ref{EstimateM2ballS}), in a dataset with 100 attributes and $M<2.7\cdot 10^6$ samples we should not be surprised to observe the linear separability of {\em each} sample from the rest of the database by the inequalities $\langle \boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_j\rangle<\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\langle\boldsymbol{x}_i,\boldsymbol{x}_i\rangle}$ ($i\neq j$) in the Mahalanobis inner product $\langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}\rangle =(\boldsymbol{x}, S^{-1}\boldsymbol{y})$, where $S$ is the empirical covariance matrix. The Mahalanobis inner product is used for `whitening', i.e. for transformation of the data cloud into the spherical form. Of course, these attributes should not be highly correlated and the empiric covariance matrix should be invertible.
nodes.statement_short: In data with 100 weakly correlated attributes and $M<2.7\cdot10^6$ samples, each sample is expected to be separable from the rest after whitening.

nodes.name: Separation of two random sets
nodes.statement: The question of generalisability of this correction is of great practical importance. It leads to a problem of {\em separation of two random sets}.

nodes.name: Separating a point set from a small random set via a quotient space
nodes.statement: A simple series of generalisations can be immediately produced from Theorems 1-3 for separation of an $M$-element random set $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ from a $k$-element one $\{\boldsymbol{y}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{y}_k\}$ for $k<n$. For this purpose, we can consider a linear space $E=\mathrm{span}\{\boldsymbol{y}_i-\boldsymbol{y}_1 \, | \, i=2,\ldots , k\}$ and study separation of a point from an $M$-element set in the projection onto the quotient space $\mathbb{R}^{n}/E$. If ${\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_k}$ are independent then separation would likely be limited to sets of small cardinality $k<n$. If, in contrast, ${\boldsymbol{y}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_k}$ are pair-wise positively correlated then we can expect that a single functional would separate them from $S$, with reasonable probability even for some $k\geq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Separate an $M$-set from a $k$-set ($k<n$) by projecting onto $\mathbb{R}^n/E$ with $E$ spanned by differences of the $y_i$.

nodes.name: Extreme selectivity of neuron models
nodes.statement: If we accept that a) linear functionals followed by nonlinear threshold-modulated response as phenomenological models of cells whose activity was measured, b) the number of inputs converging to these cells is large enough, and c) they are statistically independent, then extreme selectivity of responses of such models follows immediately from Theorem 2.
assumptions: a) linear functionals followed by nonlinear threshold-modulated response as phenomenological models of cells whose activity was measured
b) the number of inputs converging to these cells is large enough
conclusions: extreme selectivity of responses of such models follows immediately from Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Set $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ and compute $E[\overline Y]=R^2/n$, minimal $R_0^2$
nodes.statement: Let us take $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$. Consider the centres located in the cube, $0\leq c_i \leq 1$. Then $0\leq Y_i \leq 1$ and $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R^2$. In particular, if $c_i=\overline{X}_i$ then $\mathbf{E}\left [\overline Y \right]=\frac{1}{n}R_0^2$ (the minimal possible value), where $R_0^2=\sum_i \sigma_i^2\geq n\sigma_0^2$. In general, $n\sigma_0^2\leq R^2 \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $Y_i=(X_i-c_i)^2$ and compute $E[\overline Y]=R^2/n$, minimal $R_0^2$

nodes.name: Hoeffding: a point lies in the spherical layer (9)
nodes.statement: With probability $p>1- 2\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ a random point $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to the spherical layer ($\delta={nt}/{R_0^2}$, $t=\delta R_0^2/n$): \begin{equation} 1-\delta \leq {\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2}/{R_0^2}\leq 1+\delta. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Hoeffding: a point lies in the spherical layer (9)

nodes.name: Union bound: all $M$ points in the layer; reduce to the Fig. 1 picture
nodes.statement: Consider $M$ i.i.d. points $\{\boldsymbol{x}_1, \ldots , \boldsymbol{x}_M\}$ from the product distribution. With probability $p>1- 2M\exp \left(-2nt^2 \right)$ they all belong to the spherical layer (\ref{sphericLayer}). Therefore, with this probability we return to the situation presented in Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls} with internal radius $\sqrt{1-\delta}R_0$ and external radius $\sqrt{1+\delta}R_0$. The difference from the equidistribution in the ball is that the volume of the ball is concentrated near the external sphere, while the distribution in the layer (\ref{sphericLayer}) is concentrated around the sphere $\|\boldsymbol{x}-\overline{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^2=R_0^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound: all $M$ points in the layer; reduce to the Fig. 1 picture

nodes.name: Hoeffding again: a point avoids the separating ball $B$
nodes.statement: The radius of ball $B$ is defined by $\rho^2=(1+\delta)R_0^2-(1-\delta)R_0^2=2\delta R_0^2$. The concentration radius (\ref{ConcRad}) for the spheres concentric with the ball $B$ (Fig.~\ref{Fig:Balls}) is defined by $R^2=R_0^2+(1-\delta)R_0^2=(2-\delta)R_0^2$. Therefore, a random point does not belong to the ball $B$ with probability $p>1- \exp \left(-2n\tau^2 \right)$, where $\tau=\frac{1}{n}(R^2-\rho^2)=\frac{1}{n}(2-3 \delta)R^2_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Hoeffding again: a point avoids the separating ball $B$

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Thus, we get the following statement.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude Theorem 2
